summary: Defines criteria for designing an Autonomous System Border Router that runs BGP4 or IDRP for IP with external routers and OSPF as its internal protocol. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1745 sets out how a border router should translate routes when it speaks BGP or IDRP to the networks outside and OSPF to the networks inside. The two protocols name things differently and use different scales for cost, so the memo says which fields correspond, what must be filtered out, and how the OSPF route tag is used to remember where a route came from.

questions: how does bgp interact with ospf
what is an autonomous system border router
what is the ospf external route tag
subtitle: The rules a border router follows when it moves routes between OSPF inside and BGP outside its network.

tldr.problem: A router at the edge of an autonomous system speaks an exterior protocol, BGP4 or IDRP, to other networks and an interior protocol, OSPF, to its own. The two protocols describe routes differently, so something has to say how one set of fields becomes the other.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the mapping in both directions, using the 32-bit OSPF external route tag to carry the information needed to set the BGP ORIGIN and PATH attributes. It also requires the BGP identifier to be the same as the OSPF router ID, so a border router can work out which of its neighbours a route came through.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1745 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a standards track specification, and it also documents a forwarding loop that two protocols can both behave correctly into, and which the rule about merging equal cost paths into a set is there to prevent.

facts.label: Default OSPF metric type on import

today: RFC 1745 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a standards track specification of how a border router should exchange routes between BGP4 or IDRP outside its autonomous system and OSPF inside it, and it has not been obsoleted by a later RFC.

sections.title: What This Document Decides
sections.content:
The memo defines the criteria to be used when designing an Autonomous System Border Router, an ASBR, that runs BGP4 or IDRP for IP with other ASBRs outside the autonomous system and OSPF as its interior gateway protocol. IDRP came out of the same work as BGP and may be considered a follow-on to BGP-3 and BGP-4, so most fields defined in the interaction between them are named the same; where they differ, the IDRP fields are shown separately. The IDRP RD_PATH and RD_SET fields serve the same purpose as the BGP AS_PATH and AS_SET fields, and this document uses the terms PATH and SET for whichever is in play.

The fields that correspond are the BGP and IDRP MULTI_EXIT_DISC, the BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH or AS_SET against the OSPF tag, the IDRP EXT_INFO and RD_PATH or RD_SET, the BGP and IDRP NEXT_HOP against the OSPF Forwarding Address, and the BGP and IDRP LOCAL_PREF against the OSPF cost and type.

Two terms are defined at the start. An Autonomous System is used in the sense of the BGP RFC: even when several interior protocols and metrics are used, the administration of an AS appears to other ASs to have a single coherent interior routing plan, and from the standpoint of exterior routing an AS can be viewed as monolithic. A Routing Domain is a collection of routers which coordinate their routing knowledge using a single instance of a routing protocol. By definition a Routing Domain forms a single Autonomous System, but an Autonomous System may be composed of a collection of Routing Domains.

The document follows the conventions of the Host Requirements RFCs for the words MUST, SHOULD and MAY, and sets out a minimal implementation: it must not advertise a route containing a set of reachable destinations when none of the destinations in the address and mask pair is reachable via OSPF, it must merge the PATH into a SET when multiple exit points exist within the same autonomous system for the same external destination, and it must set the OSPF tag accurately. That subset is chosen so as to cause minimal havoc to the Internet at large, and it is strongly recommended that implementors do more than the minimum.

The document also lists what changed from the earlier BGP and OSPF interaction document. The use of the word route has a more complicated structure in BGP4, reachability exchange is updated to handle variable length net mask information, the previous BGP3 term INTER_AS_METRIC has become MULTI_EXIT_DISC, the default metric for importing BGP information into the OSPF Routing Domain is now the LOCAL_PREF attribute instead of a constant value, and BGP4 requires the ASBR to merge the paths through equal cost multipath neighbours into sets.
sections.plainLanguage: A border router runs two routing protocols at once, so the routes it learns on one side have to be described in the words of the other side. This document fixes that correspondence, defines two terms the rest of the text depends on, and states the smallest set of rules an implementation must follow to avoid breaking the wider network.

sections.title: Exporting OSPF Routes and Importing BGP Routes
sections.content:
Exporting OSPF information into BGP or IDRP has several requirements. The administrator must be able to selectively export address and mask pairs, with a filter mechanism that works at the granularity of a single pair, and the administrator must be able to filter on the OSPF tag and its sub-fields. That filter is the primary method of aggregating OSPF internal and type 1 and type 2 external routes into BGP or IDRP. The default must be to export no routes at all, with a single configuration parameter allowed to export all OSPF inter-area and intra-area pairs, and OSPF external pairs of type 1 and type 2 must never be exported unless they are explicitly configured. A pair with a non-contiguous mask must not be exported. When a pair is exported, the router may advertise it as soon as at least one of its destinations is reachable via OSPF, and must stop advertising it when none of them is. The administrator must be able to set the MULTI_EXIT_DISC attribute statically for any route, with a default of omitting it, and there must be a mechanism for a minimum delay between learning a pair via OSPF and advertising it to external neighbours, whose default value is 0. LOCAL_PREF is not used when exporting, as it is not applicable.

Importing BGP or IDRP information into OSPF has its own requirements. Implementations should let an AS control which announcements are imported, at the granularity of a single destination and also of an autonomous system, whether the originating or the adjacent one. The default must be to import nothing, with administrators configuring every destination they want. The administrator must be able to configure the OSPF cost and metric type of every imported destination, and the metric type must default to type 2. If the LOCAL_PREF value is used to construct the OSPF cost, one must be extremely careful, because in OSPF the lower cost is preferred while in BGP and IDRP the higher LOCAL_PREF is preferred, and because the OSPF cost ranges between 1 and 2^24 while LOCAL_PREF ranges between 0 and 2^32. Information learned from peers within the same AS must not be imported into OSPF, and the ASBR must never generate a default destination into the OSPF routing domain unless explicitly configured to do so. The recommended way to originate a default destination is to let the administrator specify a set of tuples of reachable destinations, PATH, default cost and default type, and generate the default when the router learns of at least one of those destinations with the corresponding PATH. MULTI_EXIT_DISC is not used when importing, as it is not applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing moves between the two protocols unless an administrator asks for it: the default is to export nothing and to import nothing, and both directions are filtered. The rules also fix which attributes survive the trip. The exterior cost and preference attributes do not carry over in either direction, and when the local preference is used to build the interior cost, the two scales and their opposite preferences have to be handled with care.

sections.title: The BGP Identifier and the OSPF Router ID
sections.content:
The BGP or IDRP identifier must be the same as the OSPF router ID at all times that the router is up. BGP4 requires that the BGP identifier be an address assigned to the BGP speaker. IDRP does not explicitly carry the identity of its speaker, but an implicit notion of it can be obtained by examining the source address in the IP packets carrying the IDRP information, so all IDRP speakers taking part in OSPF must bind the IDRP identifier to the address of the OSPF router ID. This makes it convenient for an administrator looking at a border router to correlate BGP and OSPF information based on the identifier.

The more important reason is the following scenario. Three border routers, RT1, RT2 and RT3, belong to the same autonomous system, which runs OSPF. Both RT1 and RT2 can reach an external destination X and import that information into the OSPF routing domain, and RT3 is advertising this information about X to other external BGP or IDRP speakers. RT3 must determine which border routers it is using to reach X by matching the OSPF router ID for its route to the destination with the BGP identifier of those routers, or the IP source address of the IDRP protocol packet from them. If RT3 has equal cost routes to X through RT1 and RT2, it must merge the PATH through RT1 and RT2 into a SET. Otherwise it may merge them. It may then generate the corresponding network layer reachability information for further advertisement to external peers.

The appendix works through an example of what happens when this rule is not applied. Given the domains X, A, B, C and S, with A and C running OSPF and the border routers A3 and C3 having equal cost multipath routes to A1 and A2 and to C1 and C2 respectively, domain B advertises to A the path B,X; ASBR A3 in domain A advertises the path A,B,X to domain C at ASBR C2; domain C then has two equal cost paths to X, one direct C,X and another through A, C,A,B,X; BR C3 in domain C advertises to A2 the path C,X; and domain A has two equal cost paths to X, A,C,X and A,B,X. Since A3 and C3 see equal cost routes to X through A1, A2 and C1, C2, a stable loop through the border routers A3, A2, C3, C2, A3 exists. Requiring the paths to be aggregated into sets constrains the BGP or IDRP speaker in either domain from choosing multiple routes to X and importing only one into OSPF, which breaks the multiple paths seen in one domain, and the exact domain in which they are broken is nondeterministic.
sections.plainLanguage: The border router must use the same identifier for both protocols, so that an administrator can line up the two views of the same router and so that one border router can recognise which neighbour a route arrived from. That last part matters when two neighbours offer the same route at the same cost: the paths through them have to be merged into a set, otherwise, as the appendix shows, the two networks can each advertise a route through the other and packets can loop between them for ever.

sections.title: The OSPF Tag as a Carrier for ORIGIN and PATH
sections.content:
The OSPF external route tag is a 32-bit field attached to each external route, which may be used to communicate information between AS boundary routers, with the precise nature of that information outside the scope of the OSPF specification. This document uses that field to set the ORIGIN and PATH attributes in BGP and IDRP, which are well-known mandatory attributes there. Every combination of tag bits is described in two parts: import, which says when an ASBR imports an AS external link state advertisement into the OSPF domain with that tag setting, and export, which says how the path attributes should be formatted when the ASBR exports a type 1 or type 2 OSPF external route.

The high bit of the tag is the Automatic bit. Setting it indicates that the tag was generated automatically by an ASBR; when the network administrator configures the tag it must be 0, which is the default setting. The remaining bits of an automatically generated tag are a Completeness bit, set when the ORIGIN of the route is either EGP or IGP, two bits of PathLength information, twelve bits of ArbitraryTag information that default to 0 but can be configured to anything else, and sixteen bits of AutonomousSystem number, zero if the reachable destinations are to be considered part of the local AS. A manually configured tag has the Automatic bit at zero and a 31-bit LocalInfo field, and is the default setting for importing destinations for backward compatibility with deployed implementations of OSPF; nothing must be inferred about the characteristics of the reachable destinations corresponding to it, and the route should be exported with ORIGIN set to EGP and PATH set to the local AS.

The six automatic settings are then spelled out. With Complete 0 and PathLength 00, the destinations come from routing protocols with incomplete path information that cannot carry the neighbour AS or AS path; they should be exported with ORIGIN set to EGP and PATH set to the local AS. With Complete 0 and PathLength 01, the neighbour AS is carried in the routing information, and the route should be exported with ORIGIN set to EGP and PATH set to the local AS and the next hop AS. With Complete 0 and PathLength 10, the path information is truncated, and the route must never be exported into BGP or IDRP. With Complete 1 and PathLength 00, the path information is complete, and the route should be exported with ORIGIN set to IGP and PATH set to the local AS. With Complete 1 and PathLength 01, the path information is complete and the next hop AS is known, and the route should be exported with ORIGIN set to IGP and PATH set to the local AS and the next hop AS. With Complete 1 and PathLength 10, the path information is complete and carries the AS path, and the route must not be exported into BGP or IDRP, because these destinations were already imported from BGP or IDRP into the OSPF domain and the assumption is that the BGP speaker will convey them to other BGP speakers inside the autonomous system; an ASBR learning such a destination must wait for the BGP update from its internal neighbours before advertising it to external peers. The value PathLength 11 is reserved during automatic tag generation; routers must not generate it and ASBRs must ignore tags that indicate it.
sections.plainLanguage: The 32-bit tag that OSPF already attaches to an external route is used to remember where that route came from, so that the right ORIGIN and PATH can be produced when the route is advertised outside. The top bit says whether the tag was generated by the router or typed in by an administrator. The next bit says whether the path information is complete, and two bits say how much of it survived. Two of the six automatic settings forbid exporting the route outside altogether, because the path it describes was truncated or because it came from BGP in the first place.

sections.title: The Forwarding Address and the NEXT_HOP Attribute
sections.content:
Forwarding addresses are used to avoid extra hops between multiple routers that share a common network and that speak different routing protocols with each other on that network. Both BGP and IDRP and OSPF have equivalents: in BGP and IDRP the NEXT_HOP attribute is a well-known mandatory attribute, and OSPF has a Forwarding address field.

The example given has four routers. RT1 and RT2 are in one autonomous system and RT3 and RT4 in another. RT1 and RT3 speak BGP or IDRP with each other, and RT3 and RT4 speak OSPF with each other, over a common network. When importing a reachable destination from BGP or IDRP into OSPF, RT3 must always fill the OSPF Forwarding Address with the BGP or IDRP NEXT_HOP attribute for that destination. When exporting a set of reachable destinations internal to the OSPF routing domain from OSPF to BGP or IDRP, if all the destinations in the set are reachable through RT4, then RT3 may fill the NEXT_HOP attribute with the address of RT4, to avoid requiring packets to take an extra hop through RT3 when crossing the AS boundary. This is similar to the concept of indirect neighbour support in EGP.
sections.plainLanguage: When a route crosses the border, the address of the router that should forward it is written into the receiving protocol. Coming in, the border router copies the exterior next hop into the interior forwarding address. Going out, it may name the interior router that holds the route, so that traffic does not have to pass back through the border router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has a Security Considerations section, and its entire content is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

Nothing in the document describes authentication, access control or confidentiality for the route exchanges it defines, and the rules it gives are about the shape of the routing information rather than who is allowed to send it.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed, so nothing in it should be read as a claim that the exchanges are protected.

fields.name: Automatic
fields.desc: Set when the tag was generated by an ASBR rather than typed in.

fields.name: Complete
fields.desc: Set when the ORIGIN of the route is either EGP or IGP.

fields.name: Path Length
fields.desc: Path length information; 11 is reserved and must not be generated.

fields.name: Arbitrary Tag
fields.desc: Tag information. Defaults to 0 but can be configured to anything else.

fields.name: Autonomous System
fields.desc: AS number of the reachable destinations, 0 for the local AS.

items.label: Complete 0, PathLength 10
items.desc: Path truncated. Must never be exported into BGP/IDRP.

items.label: Complete 1, PathLength 00
items.desc: Export with ORIGIN set to IGP, PATH set to the local AS.

items.label: Complete 1, PathLength 01
items.desc: Export with ORIGIN set to IGP, PATH set to the local AS and the next hop AS.

items.label: Complete 1, PathLength 10
items.desc: Already imported from BGP/IDRP. Must not be exported into BGP/IDRP.

items.label: PathLength 11
items.desc: Reserved. Must not be generated, and must be ignored on receipt.
